implementation_notes: Java's ecosystem provides the pattern as a first-class EIP element: Spring Integration's RecipientListRouter sends each message to a list of channels, its Java DSL (routeToRecipients / <recipient-list-router>) configures recipients declaratively, and RecipientListRouterManagement exposes addRecipient/removeRecipient over the control bus or JMX so the list really is data at runtime. Send timeout, ignore-send-failures and apply-sequence make the per-recipient failure policy explicit rather than accidental. Reach for the plain JDK only when a full integration framework is already too much machinery; then ExecutorService/CompletableFuture with a dedicated pool is the manual realization.
pitfalls: A router that resolves no recipient throws MessageDeliveryException unless a defaultOutputChannel (or nullChannel, to drop silently) is configured.
ignoreSendFailures=true hides a dead recipient from the caller; pair it with an error channel or message history, or the loss is invisible.
Recipients added at runtime through RecipientListRouterManagement are not shared across a clustered deployment by themselves; the list lives in the instance unless the change is distributed.

variants.name: Apache Camel recipientList EIP
variants.implementation_notes: Camel's recipientList computes the destinations from an expression (header, body, XPath, bean method) whose result may be a Collection, array, Iterator, NodeList or delimited String of endpoint URIs, then sends the same message to each - sequentially by default, concurrently with parallelProcessing and a thread pool. stopOnException selects fail-fast, an AggregationStrategy merges replies, and the allowedSchemes option restricts which URI schemes a dynamic recipient may resolve to. Choose it when routing lives in a Camel route; the Spring Integration router is the counterpart when the stack is Spring Integration.
variants.code_sketch:
from("jms:queue:orders")
    .recipientList(header("recipients"))    // Collection/array/iterator or comma-separated URIs
        .delimiter(",")
        .parallelProcessing()               // sequential by default
        .stopOnException();                 // fail-fast instead of continuing
pitfalls: The expression result must be iterable in Camel's sense; anything else is treated as a single endpoint, so a mistyped header quietly becomes a one-recipient list.
Each distinct endpoint URI resolved dynamically bypasses the producer cache (cacheSize) unless it is reused, which costs connections under high recipient churn.
A message-derived recipient list should be constrained with allowedSchemes; otherwise the producer chooses the protocol as well as the destination.

variants.name: Plain JDK fan-out with CompletableFuture and a dedicated executor
variants.idiom_name: CompletableFuture.allOf over a computed recipient list
variants.implementation_notes: Without an integration framework the pattern is a computed collection plus a completion barrier: map every recipient to CompletableFuture.runAsync(deliver, pool) and await CompletableFuture.allOf(...). This is the manual realization - there is no EIP component, no sequence stamping and no management operations, so the per-recipient error policy and the recipient data source are entirely yours. Choose it for a library or service that must not pull in Spring Integration or Camel; prefer the framework variants whenever routing configuration, message history and control-bus operations are wanted.
pitfalls: allOf(...).join() throws a single CompletionException while the other sends keep running - a per-recipient outcome map is required for honest reporting.
runAsync without an executor uses the shared ForkJoinPool.commonPool(); blocking sends there starve unrelated parallel work in the same JVM.
Virtual threads (Java 21+) make blocking sends cheap, but an unbounded fan-out still multiplies downstream load, so the recipient count must be capped regardless of thread cost.
